docs.title: JamTabaYUP
docs.text: JamTabaYUP lets you play music live with musicians anywhere in the world over NINJAM servers. It runs as a standalone app, or as an AU, VST3 or CLAP plugin inside your DAW, on macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows.

docs.title: How NINJAM jamming works
docs.text:
Over the internet, sound always arrives late, too late for playing in time together the usual way. NINJAM turns the delay into part of the music:

  • The server sets a tempo (BPM) and a loop length in beats (BPI, beats per interval). Together they make an interval, for example 16 beats at 120 BPM, 8 seconds.
  • While you play an interval, JamTabaYUP records it and streams it to the others. You hear what everyone else played in the interval before, lined up with your beat.
  • So everyone plays along with everyone else, one interval behind. It suits music built from repeating forms: blues choruses, grooves, chord loops, jams.

You hear yourself live, through your interface, your DAW or JamTabaYUP's own monitoring. A metronome keeps everyone on the same grid.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Install JamTabaYUP.
  2. Join your first jam.
  3. Learn the jam room.

JamTabaYUP is a new, open-source implementation inspired by JamTaba 2. See what's different.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
You need CMake 3.31 or later, plus Xcode's command line tools on macOS or Visual Studio 2022 (or its Build Tools) with the C++ workload on Windows.

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/jbaylies/JamTabaYUP.git

cd JamTabaYUP && cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build -j

For a universal macOS build, add -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES="arm64;x86_64". On Windows, configure with -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 and build with cmake --build build --config Release --parallel.

The first configure downloads YUP's dependencies (SDL, the plugin SDKs). Builds install the VST3 and CLAP plugins into your per-user plugin folders; pass -DJAMTABA_INSTALL_PLUGINS=OFF to skip that.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
folder contents source/engine The NINJAM client with no GUI: protocol, connection thread, Vorbis, the real-time audio engine. source/plugin The audio processor, the session model, saved settings. source/ui The window: server browser, jam room, widgets. tools/ninjam_cli A command-line client and self-tests. tools/test-server A config for a local NINJAM server. scripts Release packaging. docs This manual.

PORTING_PLAN.md describes the design and the state of each part.

docs.title: Testing the engine
docs.text:
ninjam_cli runs the engine with a simulated audio device:

build/ninjam_cli selftest

build/ninjam_cli servers

For full sessions, build Cockos ninjamsrv (source, ninjam/server) and run it from tools/test-server with ninjamsrv-test.cfg. Then connect two clients, one sending a tone and one checking it hears it:

build/ninjam_cli connect localhost:20490 --name alice --tone 440 --seconds 30

build/ninjam_cli connect localhost:20490 --name bob --no-transmit --seconds 25 --expect-tone 440

To show the room browser and globe with made-up rooms, point JAMTABA_SERVER_LIST at a local list such as tools/test-server/servers-sample.json. The globe's land data is generated by tools/world/make_world_data.py from Natural Earth.

To open the standalone app straight into a room, set JAMTABA_CONNECT (and optionally JAMTABA_NAME) before launching it:

JAMTABA_CONNECT=localhost:20490 JAMTABA_NAME=me build/JamTabaYUP.app/Contents/MacOS/JamTabaYUP

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Releases are built locally, on macOS and on Windows:

  1. scripts/package_release.sh on the Mac.
  2. scripts\package_release.ps1 on Windows.
  3. Copy the Windows build-release\stage folder to build-release/win-stage on the Mac.
  4. scripts/make_release_zips.sh writes both zips to build-release/dist.

docs.title: The manual
docs.text:
The manual is built with MkDocs and the Material theme, from docs/ and mkdocs.yml:

pip install mkdocs mkdocs-material && mkdocs serve

mkdocs gh-deploy publishes it to the gh-pages branch.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
Type in the box at the bottom of the chat panel and press Enter. The panel shows:

  • messages, with the sender's name in teal,
  • private messages, marked "(private)",
  • the server's own messages and the topic, in orange,
  • people joining and leaving, tempo changes and connection status, in grey.

Scroll up to read older messages. Chat in the top bar hides or shows the panel.

docs.title: Chord progressions
docs.text:
To share the changes of a tune, post them in chat with a bar line between measures:

| Am7 | D7 | Gmaj7 | Cmaj7 |

JamTabaYUP shows the measures above the beat bar, spread across the interval, and lights the measure being played. With 16 beats per interval and four measures, each measure covers four beats.

A measure can hold several chords, separated by spaces: | C Am | F G |. Chord symbols such as F#m7b5, Bbmaj7/D, G7(b9), Dsus4, N.C. and % (repeat) are understood. A line with anything that isn't a chord between the bars is treated as an ordinary message. The latest progression posted stays until someone posts another.

docs.title: Credits and license
docs.text: JamTabaYUP is free software: you can redistribute it and modify it under the terms of the GNU General Public License, version 2 or (at your option) any later version.

docs.title: Thanks to
docs.text:
• JamTaba 2, by Elieser de Jesus and contributors, whose workflow and layout JamTabaYUP follows. JamTaba carries no license, so none of its code, artwork or text is used here.
  • NINJAM, by Cockos Incorporated. The protocol code follows the NINJAM source (GPL-2.0-or-later).
  • YUP (ISC), the framework JamTabaYUP is built with, and the libraries it brings: SDL3, the VST3, CLAP and AudioUnit SDKs, Rive, HarfBuzz and more.
  • libogg and libvorbis, by the Xiph.Org Foundation (BSD), for the audio NINJAM sends.
  • ninbot.com, whose server list powers the room browser and the globe.
  • Natural Earth (public domain), for the land outlines on the globe.

Each release zip includes THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt with the full license of every library built into JamTabaYUP.

docs.title: Differences from JamTaba 2
docs.text: JamTabaYUP takes its workflow and layout from JamTaba 2: a browser of public rooms, then a jam room with your channel, everyone else's strips, the interval progress and chat. It isn't a port of JamTaba's code. JamTaba carries no license, so JamTabaYUP was written from scratch on YUP, with its network code following Cockos NINJAM.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• A GPU-drawn interface that stays sharp on Retina and high-DPI displays.
  • CLAP and VST3 plugins on macOS, alongside AU; VST3 and CLAP on Windows.
  • Universal macOS builds for Apple Silicon and Intel.

docs.title: Left out on purpose
docs.text: JamTaba 2 feature in JamTabaYUP The looper (recording and replaying intervals) Not included. Hosting VST/AU plugins inside the standalone app Not included: use the plugin version in a DAW for effects. Video (camera streaming) Not included. Multitrack recording of jams, Reaper project export Not included: record the plugin's output in your DAW. Built-in private server Not included: run Cockos ninjamsrv. Listening to a room's stream before joining Not included. MIDI sync out Not included. Voice chat channels Received channels in voice-chat mode aren't played. Several local channels and subchannels One local channel for now. Themes, translations One theme, English only. Country flags from IP addresses Not included. ASIO on Windows Not yet: Windows Audio (WASAPI) only.

docs.title: Nobody hears me
docs.text:
• Is XMIT lit on your strip? It takes effect at the next interval.
  • Does your meter move when you play? If not, check the input: in the app, Settings at the top of the window and the input button on your strip; in a DAW, the track's input.
  • On macOS, has the app been allowed to use the microphone? See System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone.
  • Is your channel muted (M)? Mute silences what you send too.

docs.title: I can't hear someone
docs.text:
• Is their RX on and their channel not muted? Is someone else soloed?
  • Does their line flash green each interval? If not, nothing is arriving: they may not be transmitting.
  • They may have only just joined: a channel starts at the next interval.

docs.title: I hear myself twice, or with an echo
docs.text: Turn off MON if your interface or DAW already monitors your input.

docs.title: The others say I'm late
docs.text: Nothing to fix: in NINJAM everyone hears everyone else one interval late, by design. Play in time with the metronome and the beat bar, and it lines up for everyone.

docs.title: The public room list is empty
docs.text: JamTabaYUP fetches it from ninbot.com every 30 seconds. If it can't, the browser says so; check your internet connection, or connect to a server by its address.

docs.title: "The server closed the connection" or "The server stopped responding"
docs.text: The server dropped you: it may be full, restarting, or your connection broke. Join again. Some servers drop you if you don't accept their licence within two minutes.

docs.title: The app doesn't open on macOS
docs.text: See Installing: the builds aren't notarized, so macOS blocks them until you clear the quarantine flag or click Open Anyway.

docs.title: Where does the globe get people's locations? Can others see mine?
docs.text: From the public server list at ninbot.com, which estimates each connected musician's rough location from their internet address and publishes it with the room. JamTabaYUP only shows what the list already publishes; it doesn't look up anyone's address itself. Anyone using a client that reads the list, JamTabaYUP or JamTaba, can see the rough location of people in public rooms, yours included. Private servers that aren't on the list don't appear.

docs.title: Can I record the jam?
docs.text: Record the plugin's output in your DAW. JamTabaYUP doesn't record by itself.

docs.title: 1. Name yourself
docs.text: When JamTabaYUP is not in a room, it shows the server browser. Type your name in the first field; the others see it next to your channel. Spaces, @ and : are removed, because NINJAM servers don't allow them. The second field names your channel, for example "guitar" or "vocals".

docs.title: 2. Pick a room
docs.text:
Public rooms lists the NINJAM servers that ninbot.com watches, refreshed every 30 seconds, busiest first. Each card shows:

  • the server address,
  • its current tempo (BPM) and interval length (BPI),
  • how many people are in it, one dot per seat, and their names.

Click a card, or its Join button, to go in.

docs.title: Who's there, on the globe
docs.text:
When the window is wide enough, a globe next to the list shows where the musicians in a room are. Point at a room to turn the globe toward its musicians: each gets a pin and a line out to their name and country. The globe turns by itself; drag it to spin it by hand.

The locations come from the public server list, which estimates each musician's area from their internet address; they're coarse, usually a city or region. Rooms whose list has no locations show none.

A room with nobody but its bot is a good place to try things out alone. A busy room is a good place to listen first: turn your XMIT off (see your channel) until you're ready to play along.

docs.title: 3. Or connect to a private server
docs.text: Type the address as host:port (for example ninbot.com:2049, or a friend's server), add a password if the server needs one, and click Connect or press Enter. Without a password, JamTabaYUP logs in anonymously, which most public servers allow.

docs.title: 4. Accept the server's licence
docs.text: Many servers show a licence agreement first: the terms of playing there, usually that sessions may be recorded or streamed. Read it, then click Accept and join or Decline.

docs.title: 5. Play
docs.text:
You're in the jam room. Listen for a few intervals to get the form of the tune, then play along. What you play reaches the others one interval later, lined up with their beat.

To leave, click Leave. If the connection drops, you're back in the browser with the reason shown above the room list.

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Download the zip for your system from the releases page:

zip contents needs JamTabaYUP-<version>-macOS.zip JamTabaYUP.app, .component (AU), .vst3, .clap macOS 11 or later, Apple Silicon or Intel JamTabaYUP-<version>-Windows-x64.zip JamTabaYUP.exe, .vst3, .clap 64-bit Windows 10 or later

Each zip has an INSTALL.txt with the same steps as this page.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Put the app anywhere, such as /Applications. For the plugins, copy each one into its folder. In Finder, use Go > Go to Folder and paste the path; create the folder if it doesn't exist.

file folder for JamTabaYUP.component ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/Components Logic, GarageBand JamTabaYUP.vst3 ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3 Ableton Live, Cubase, Reaper JamTabaYUP.clap ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/CLAP Bitwig, Reaper

The builds aren't signed with an Apple Developer ID, so macOS blocks them after download. Clear the quarantine flag once per copied file in Terminal:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/JamTabaYUP.app

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/Library/Audio/Plug-Ins/VST3/JamTabaYUP.vst3

and likewise for the .component and .clap. For the app you can instead try to open it once, then click Open Anyway in System Settings > Privacy & Security.

The first time the app uses your audio input, macOS asks for microphone access. Click Allow, or the other musicians will hear silence. You can change it later in System Settings > Privacy & Security > Microphone.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Put JamTabaYUP.exe anywhere. Copy the plugins into their folders, creating them if needed:

file folder for JamTabaYUP.vst3 (a folder: copy all of it) C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3 Ableton Live, Cubase, Reaper JamTabaYUP.clap C:\Program Files\Common Files\CLAP Bitwig, Reaper

Copying into Program Files asks for administrator rights. Without them, use %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Common\VST3 and %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Common\CLAP, though not every DAW scans those.

The app isn't code-signed, so SmartScreen warns the first time: click More info, then Run anyway. If Windows asks whether JamTabaYUP may use the network, allow it.

docs.title: Choosing your audio interface (standalone app)
docs.text: Click Settings at the top of the window, choose your audio interface, its inputs and outputs, and the smallest buffer size that plays without crackles. On Windows the app uses Windows Audio (WASAPI); ASIO isn't supported yet.

docs.title: The jam room
docs.text: From top to bottom:

docs.title: Top bar
docs.text:
• Server and topic: the address you're on, how many people are in it, and the server's topic.
  • BPM and BPI: the server's tempo and interval length, with arrows and a Vote button for proposing a change. See tempo and voting.
  • Metronome: its volume, and M to mute it.
  • Master: the volume of everything JamTabaYUP plays, with a level meter.
  • Chat: shows or hides the chat panel.
  • Leave: disconnects and goes back to the server browser.

docs.title: Beat bar
docs.text:
One block per beat of the interval. Beats already played are dim, and the beat in progress fills as it goes. Beat 1 is where each interval starts: what the others played in the last interval begins again here.

When someone posts a chord progression in chat, its measures appear above the beats. See chat and chord progressions.

docs.title: Your channel
docs.text: On the left: what you send, and how you hear yourself. See your channel.

docs.title: Other musicians
docs.text: In the middle, one coloured group per musician, with a strip for each channel they send. Scroll sideways with the mouse wheel or trackpad when there are more than fit. See other musicians.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
On the right: messages, the topic, people joining and leaving, and tempo changes. Type in the box at the bottom and press Enter.

The window can be resized; the strips and chat make room.

docs.title: Other musicians
docs.text:
Each musician in the room gets a coloured group with their name on top and one strip per channel they send (some send several, for example guitar and voice).

control what it does RX Receive. Turn it off to stop downloading this channel: it saves bandwidth, and the channel goes silent. M, S Mute this channel, or solo it (only soloed channels are heard, yours included). fader This channel's volume in your mix. Double-click for 0 dB. meter The channel's level as you hear it. pan Where you hear the channel, left to right. line at the bottom Flashes green each time a whole interval from this channel has arrived.

Your mix of each musician (volume, pan, mute) is remembered by name and channel, so it's back the next time you meet them.

docs.title: Why someone is silent at first
docs.text:
A channel starts playing at the start of an interval, with the interval the musician finished before it. Someone who has just joined, or just turned their transmit on, is silent for an interval or two.

If a channel's line never flashes, nothing is arriving from it: the musician isn't transmitting, or their connection can't keep up.

docs.title: In your DAW
docs.text:
The plugin has the same window as the app. Insert it as an audio effect on the track you play into (a guitar, a microphone or a synth track):

  • The track's audio is your channel: JamTabaYUP sends it to the others.
  • The plugin's output is the jam: the other musicians and the metronome, plus your own signal only if you turn MON on.

Your DAW already monitors the track, so MON starts off in the plugin.

DAW how Logic Pro Insert JamTabaYUP (AU) in an audio or instrument track's Audio FX slot. Turn on input monitoring for the track. Ableton Live Put the VST3 on an audio track with your input selected and Monitor set to In (or Auto with the track armed). Bitwig, Reaper Load the CLAP or VST3 on the track you play into. Cubase Insert the VST3 on the track and turn on its monitor button.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: NINJAM keeps its own interval clock: the server sets the tempo, and the intervals run whether or not your DAW is playing. To record a jam in your DAW, set the DAW's tempo to the room's BPM. The project's bars won't line up with the intervals unless you start recording on beat 1.

docs.title: Saved with your project
docs.text: Your name, the last server, your channel settings, the metronome and master levels, and each musician's mix are saved with the project. Reopening the project doesn't reconnect automatically: join again from the browser.

docs.title: BPM and BPI
docs.text: The server decides the tempo for everyone: BPM (beats per minute) and BPI (beats per interval). When either changes, the change takes effect at the start of the next interval, and the chat panel says so.

docs.title: The metronome
docs.text: The metronome clicks every beat, with a higher click on beat 1 of each interval. Set its volume with the Metronome fader in the top bar, or mute it with M. In the plugin, the click is mixed into the plugin's output.

docs.title: Voting for a change
docs.text:
Most servers let the people in the room vote on the tempo:

  1. Click the arrows next to BPM or BPI (or scroll on it) to choose a value. Hold Shift to step by 10. The proposed value turns teal.
  2. Click Vote.

JamTabaYUP sends the vote as a chat command, so you can also type it in chat:

!vote bpm 110
!vote bpi 16

The server changes the tempo once enough people vote for the same value, often half the room, and answers in chat. If voting is off on that server, the server says so instead.

docs.title: Your channel
docs.text:
The strip on the left is you: what you send to the others, and how you hear yourself.

control what it does input button (standalone app) In 1+2 sends inputs 1 and 2 as a stereo channel; In 1 or In 2 sends one input in mono. In the plugin, the channel is the track's audio. XMIT Transmit. When it's lit (red), what you play is sent to the others. Changes take effect at the next interval, so nobody gets half an interval. MON Monitor: hear your input through JamTabaYUP. Leave it off if your interface or DAW already lets you hear yourself, or you'll hear yourself twice. It starts on in the app and off in the plugin. M, S Mute and solo. Mute also silences what you send. fader Your level, both what you send and what you hear. Double-click for 0 dB; hold Shift for fine steps. meter Your level after the fader: the bright bar is the average (RMS), the dim bar the peaks, the thin line the recent peak. pan Where you hear yourself, left to right. It doesn't change what you send. Double-click to centre. line at the bottom The interval being recorded. Red while transmitting.

Keep your level healthy but out of the red: the others hear your channel at the level you send it.

The name under You is the channel name you typed in the server browser. It's sent to the server when you join.
